extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (aesthetics, Kantian studies)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and evaluative standards for making and assessing judgements of taste, beauty, and teleological judgement in nature and art, as presented in Kant's Critique of Judgement. Covers phenomenology of aesthetic pleasure, methodological limits for teaching art, and the role of purposiveness and teleology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empiricism vs. Rationalism of the Principle of Taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Either place the principle of taste in empirical grounds (a posteriori) — the empiricism of taste — where the Object of satisfaction does not differ from the pleasant; or concede that it judges on a priori grounds — the rationalism of taste — where, if the judgement rests on definite concepts, it tends to resemble the good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: empiricism would reduce beauty to mere pleasantness (contingent agreement like palate-taste), while strict rationalism threatens to eliminate beauty by subsuming it under determinate concepts. Kant argues there are a priori grounds of satisfaction that cannot be captured by definite concepts, so taste contains rational elements without being fully conceptual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realism vs. Idealism of Purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Within rationalism of taste, one must decide whether the purposiveness invoked is realist (objective purposiveness: nature/art actually has purposes designed for our judgement) or idealist (subjective purposiveness: purposiveness is a feature of our reflective relation to the object).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments for realism: many natural formations (flowers, plumage, shell-fish) look as if produced for our aesthetic delight. Arguments for idealism: Reason favors parsimony and nature shows mechanical tendencies producing form without invoking designed purposes. Kant favors idealism for explaining the universality and autonomy of aesthetic judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty judged by a priori subjective purposiveness (Ideality of Purposiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: In judging beauty we invariably seek its gauge in ourselves a priori, and the aesthetic judgement is legislative (it gives a law to itself) rather than being grounded in empirical instruction from nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: the judgement of taste is autonomous and not derived from empirical rules; anti-pattern is to treat the aesthetic judgement as if it were learned from nature (which would make it heteronomous and empirical). This ideality explains why aesthetic claims purport to be universally valid despite lack of determinate concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion of Beautiful Art: product of Genius, not of Understanding/Science
rubrics_metrics.description: Beautiful art, as such, must not be considered a product of Understanding and Science but of Genius; it must obtain its rule through aesthetical Ideas which differ from rational Ideas of definite purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: art governed by merely mechanical or scientifically designed purposes is only pleasant, not beautiful. Teaching art must encourage imagination and aesthetic ideas rather than formulaic application of rules. Anti-pattern: treating exemplary works as templates to be imitated stifles genius and true art.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Beautiful as Symbol of the Morally Good — immediate pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: The beautiful pleases immediately (in reflective intuition), unlike moral goodness which pleases as a concept; beauty's pleasure is direct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This immediacy distinguishes aesthetic pleasure from moral judgement's conceptual satisfaction. Evaluators should check that the pleasure ascribed to a work is immediate and not mediated by conceptual interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Beautiful as Symbol of the Morally Good — disinterestedness (pleases apart from interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty pleases apart from any interest; it is disinterested pleasure, whereas the morally good is necessarily bound up with an interest (produced by the moral judgement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for aesthetic value: the satisfaction must not be grounded in personal desires or external ends. If an appreciation depends on contingent interests, it is mere liking, not aesthetic judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Beautiful as Symbol of the Morally Good — freedom of the Imagination harmonised with Understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: In judging the beautiful, the freedom of the Imagination (and the sensibility of our faculty) is represented as harmonious with the conformity to law of the Understanding; in moral judgement the freedom of the will is thought as harmony of the will with universal laws of Reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A valid aesthetic judgement manifests a felt compatibility between imaginative play and cognitive order; works that evoke this free play in service of formal harmony satisfy this criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Beautiful as Symbol of the Morally Good — subjective universality
rubrics_metrics.description: The subjective principle in judging the beautiful is represented as universal, i.e., as claiming validity for every one, though not cognisable through any universal concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic judgements claim a non-conceptual universality: when making such judgements, the speaker expects agreement from others without offering a determinate conceptual proof. A failure to make such a presumptive claim (or explicitly grounding judgement in idiosyncratic taste) undermines the status of the judgement as 'taste.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste as faculty for judging sensible illustration of moral Ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste is a faculty for judging the sensible illustration of moral Ideas (by analogy in reflection); it allows transition from mere charm of sense to habitual moral interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations of art or natural beauty should attend to whether the work can serve as a sensible manifestation that promotes moral feeling or ideas. The propaedeutic for taste is cultivation of moral feeling and the development of moral Ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Taste: manner (modus) not method (methodus)
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be no science of the Beautiful and the judgement of taste is not determinable by principles; for beautiful art there is a manner (modus) of teaching, not a prescriptive method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: instructors should demonstrate and exemplify, using criticism to awaken the pupil's imagination and judgement, rather than attempting to teach fixed rules. Universal rules, if offered, function chiefly as mnemonic reminders, not incontrovertible prescriptions. Anti-pattern: presenting immutable rules that pupils treat as formulae, thereby stifling genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaedeutic for Taste: cultivation via humaniora and moral feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: The propaedeutic to beautiful art lies less in precepts than in the culture of mental powers by means of humaniora — developing sympathy and capacity for universal communication — and in cultivating moral Ideas and moral feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pedagogical emphasis should be on broad humanistic education and moral development to ground a shared sense of taste. Without examples and cultural continuity, later ages may lack the natural models that mediate between high culture and free nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleological Judgement as RegulativE, not Constitutive
rubrics_metrics.description: The teleological act of judgement is rightly applied problematically (regulatively) to the investigation of nature—bringing phenomena under rules by analogy with purposive causality—rather than as a constitutive principle that introduces a new causality into natural science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use teleological reasoning as an heuristic for observation and inquiry where mechanical causality does not suffice, but avoid treating teleology as an ontological claim that nature is actually governed by purposes. Constitutive teleology would improperly convert reflective judgement into determinant natural science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Formal (Intellectual) vs. Real (Material) Purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: There is objective intellectual purposiveness (formal) distinct from real material purposiveness: e.g., geometrical figures display objective purposiveness in reference to multiple problem-solutions (formal), whereas the ordered layout of a garden is empirical, real purposiveness dependent on assumed purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing purposiveness in objects, determine whether the purposiveness is a priori formal (derivable from intellectual construction, like geometry) or empirical and material (requires given objects and the concept of purpose). Admiration often arises when a manifold of rules united a priori seems to match empirically given order, making it appear purposive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Schematical vs. Symbolical Hypotyposes for Intuition of Concepts and Ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Intuitions supplied to concepts a priori are either schemata (direct a priori intuition corresponding to concepts of Understanding) or symbols (indirect intuitions analogically representing Ideas of Reason).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attempting to make rational Ideas intelligible in sensuous terms, employ symbolical hypotyposes: they provide analogous sensible presentations for reflection on non-intuitive Ideas (e.g., political states as bodies or machines). Beware conflating symbolical representation with mere signs or imitations; symbols function by analogy in the rule of reflection, not by providing direct empirical schemas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution of Antinomies via Supersensible Ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three antinomies corresponding to higher cognitive faculties (understanding, judgement, reason), and their unavoidable conflicts can be resolved by referring judgements to a supersensible substrate (manifested in three Ideas: the supersensible as substrate of nature; as principle of subjective purposiveness of nature for cognition; and as principle of purposes of freedom in moral sphere).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should recognize when contradictory claims in aesthetic or teleological reflection indicate appeal to different faculties; resolution requires positing regulative supersensible Ideas rather than attempting empirical adjudication. This provides a conceptual method for reconciling theoretical and practical antinomies in aesthetic judgement.
